beats.say: While Baghdad celebrated peace, Sultan Mesud I secretly marshaled troops near the fortress of Harput.
He aimed to cripple the Armenian lord Thoros II, whose mountain stronghold threatened Seljuk trade routes.
Under cover of night, 7,000 mounted archers slipped through the rugged Elazığ passes, unheard by scouts.
The Seljuks deployed early trebuchet prototypes, a rare technology borrowed from Crusader engineers in Antioch.
At dawn, a sudden avalanche from the nearby Munzur cliffs buried the Armenian supply wagons.
Caught without food, Thoros surrendered, and the Seljuks seized Harput, opening a corridor to Cilicia.
The victory forced the Byzantine emperor to grant the Seljuks tax-free passage across the Euphrates.
Historians once blamed a plague for the Seljuk surge, but recent tablets confirm the siege's strategic brilliance.
The captured Harput became a mint, producing silver dirhams that financed the later Battle of Myriokephalon.
Thus a hidden mountain assault in 1146 set the stage for the Seljuks' ultimate rise in Anatolia.
